{{short description|American mathematician (born 1944)|bot=PearBOT 5}}
'''Carl Bernard Pomerance''' (born 1944) is an American [[number theory|number theorist]].  He attended college at [[Brown University]] and later received his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1972 with a dissertation proving that any odd [[perfect number]] has at least seven distinct [[prime factor]]s.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=5609}}</ref> He joined the faculty at the [[University of Georgia]], becoming full professor in 1982. He subsequently worked at [[Lucent Technologies]] for a number of years, and then became a [[distinguished professor]] at [[Dartmouth College]].

==Contributions==
He has over 120 publications, including co-authorship with [[Richard Crandall]] of ''Prime numbers: a computational perspective'' ([[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]], first edition 2001, second edition 2005<ref name="Crandall">{{cite book|title=Prime numbers: a computational perspective|last1=Crandall|first1=R.|last2=Pomerance|first2=C.|publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York|year=2005|isbn=978-0-387-25282-7|edition=second|doi=10.1007/0-387-28979-8|author-link=Richard Crandall}}</ref>), and with [[Paul Erdős]].<ref name="Canfield Erdös Pomerance 1983">{{cite journal | last1=Canfield | first1=E.R | last2=Erdös | first2=Paul | last3=Pomerance | first3=Carl | title=On a problem of Oppenheim concerning "factorisatio numerorum" | journal=[[Journal of Number Theory]] | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=17 | issue=1 | year=1983 | issn=0022-314X | doi=10.1016/0022-314x(83)90002-1 | pages=1–28| doi-access=free }}</ref> He is the inventor of one of the [[integer factorization]] methods, the [[quadratic sieve]] algorithm, which was used in 1994 for the factorization of [[RSA-129]]. He is also one of the discoverers of the [[Adleman–Pomerance–Rumely primality test]].

==Awards and honors==
He has won many teaching and research awards, including the [[Chauvenet Prize]] in 1985,<ref name="Pomerance primality testing">{{cite journal | last=Pomerance | first=Carl | title=Recent developments in primality testing | journal=[[The Mathematical Intelligencer]] | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=3 | issue=3 | year=1981 | issn=0343-6993 | doi=10.1007/bf03022861 | pages=97–105| s2cid=121750836 }}</ref> the [[Deborah and Franklin Haimo Awards for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics|Deborah and Franklin Haimo Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics]] in 1997,<ref name=web>{{Cite web|url=https://maa.org/member-communities/maa-awards/teaching-awards/section-award|title=Recipients of the Deborah and Franklin Tepper Haimo Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics; Mathematical Association of America|website=www.maa.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240608175318/https://maa.org/member-communities/maa-awards/teaching-awards/section-award |archive-date=8 June 2024 }}</ref> and the [[Levi L. Conant Prize]] in 2001 for "A Tale of Two Sieves".<ref name="TaleTwoSieves">{{cite journal |last=Pomerance |first=Carl |date=December 1996 |title=A Tale of Two Sieves |journal=[[Notices of the AMS]] |volume=43 |issue=12 |pages=1473–1485}}</ref>

In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list|title=List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society|date=2017|website=www.ams.org|language=en-US|access-date=2017-06-30}}</ref> He also became the [[John G. Kemeny]] Parents Professor of Mathematics in the same year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.dartmouth.edu/news/2012/11/dartmouth-mathematicians-honored-preeminent-professional-society|title=Dartmouth Mathematicians Honored by Preeminent Professional Society {{!}} Dartmouth News|last=Blumberg|first=Joseph|date=2012-11-08|website=Dartmouth News|language=en|access-date=2017-06-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/cv15page1.pdf|title=Curriculum Vitae|last=Pomerance|first=Carl|access-date=30 June 2017}}</ref>
